#59. I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
📖 Baca

I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Entrepreneur)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary.
  • After it started, creative quality dropped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

Industry observers note that the target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those demonstrates up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

For a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

Sources indicate that we traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

When we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. Newly introduced editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

Industry observers note that that changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

In a recent development, A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

According to recent reports, bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

We stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

According to recent reports, the results came promptly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

It has been revealed that the difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

In a recent development, we’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

The early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

While the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

The hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Sources indicate that before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

If you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

It has been revealed that the bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

Recent findings suggest that the target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

  • In a recent development, like the previous compilation of classic skateboarding games, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4 remakes the classic third and fourth games in the series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PlayStation has revealed this month's batch of free games for PlayStation Plus subscribers. All PS Plus members will be able to claim a trio of freebies starting December 1--Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4, Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2, and Amnesia: The Bunker. If you haven't claimed November's PlayStation Plus free games yet, make sure to do so before next Tuesday. Like the previous compilation of classic skateboarding games, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4 remakes the classic third and fourth games in the series. With enhanced visuals, familiar gameplay, and a killer soundtrack, it also adds extra content to the mix--and yes, the soundtrack still slaps. While Dragon Ball Xenoverse 3 won't be out until late next year, don't sleep on the first sequel. It's still a solid action-RPG where you craft your own custom fighter to join Trunks and the Time Squad, and it received a ton of post-launch support that stretched for years. The game also received a free current-gen revision in 2024, sharpening its visuals for modern systems. Finally, Amnesia: The Bunker is a pretty great horror game to play in case you need to escape all the festive season cheer. As French soldier Henri Clément, trench warfare takes on a terrifying fresh form as you're hunted by sinister forces in the shadows, and the game keeps you on your toes as you try to escape the battlefields of World War 1 in one piece. #56. Breaking: AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4861 w)

Breaking: AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang is back at Nvidia.
  • According to recent reports, jensen Huang is back at Nvidia.
  • Investors may be relieved to have Huang back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the tech giant into a leadership crisis. Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board stated it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has announced additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns. Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him. Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN. The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses. Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait? Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it. “AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.” AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology. THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker. Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise? Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players. “Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub states. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.” Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products. “The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.” That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on. In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan showed how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve customers as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices. Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing. “The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says. She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning. “I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says. For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations. Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance. THE BILL IS COMING DUE Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology. Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more quickly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save. “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.” Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive. Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost. Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified. The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive. Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with. “Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company. This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each newly introduced generation of frontier models? Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow. “I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.” WHO GETS THE VALUE? Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software. Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods. “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.” His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient. “Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?” Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work. “These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says. Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify. For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most crucial operations. “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary. A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running. And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want. During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.” He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them. WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money. O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models. “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.” But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves. Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies. Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward. AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses. “We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns. Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed. For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them. Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology.

Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The firm closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker.

Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise?

Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players.

“Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub claims. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.”.

Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products.

Industry observers note that “The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.”.

That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the firm is betting on.

In a recent analysis for Fast Tech giant, Mark Sullivan demonstrated how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve users as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices.

Sources indicate that complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing.

“The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe indicates.

She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning.

“I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she indicates.

For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations.

Recent findings suggest that now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance.

Industry observers note that investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology.

Industry observers note that kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management tech giant Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more rapidly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save.

In a recent development, “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley indicates. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.”.

Recent findings suggest that businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive.

Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost.

Recent findings suggest that some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified.

Industry observers note that the company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can swiftly become expensive.

Industry observers note that airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with.

“Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Firm.

This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each new generation of frontier models?

It has been revealed that companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow.

“I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.”.

Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software.

Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods.

According to recent reports, “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he states. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.”.

In a recent development, his organization combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient.

Industry observers note that “Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen indicates. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?”.

Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work.

“These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says.

Sources indicate that consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify.

For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most important operations.

According to recent reports, “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary.

A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running.

And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want.

During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.”.

He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them.

A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money.

O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models.

“For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she indicates. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.”.

But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a tech giant can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves.

Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies.

Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward.

AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses.

“We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns.

Recent findings suggest that huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the firm with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed.

For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them.

Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

Latest Update: Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (TechCrunch)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself?
  • Now, the organization has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business.
  • Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.

Now, the organization has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman, who’s right now head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.

In a recent development, “We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano said. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.

The team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.

Recent findings suggest that the startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.

Presently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.

Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.

Supertake’s consumers’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s presently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.

For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.

Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.

“We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he notes. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he claims.

Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election.

“We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today. But that being noted, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.

It has been revealed that to address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team states it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits. For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent. There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials.

“We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” claims Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing. And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.”.

In a recent development, access to Supertake is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders noted they’ve put their money where their mouths are. Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.

Mignano, meanwhile, indicates he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.

Recent findings suggest that with the upcoming funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others. Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times. The team states it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.

Another Gaming Console Price Hike Could Be Coming, Thanks To New Tariffs

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Gamespot)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US government has unveiled a fresh round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • Industry observers note that the US government has revealed a new round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • What does this mean for gaming hardware?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US government has unveiled a fresh round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners. Under the proposed tariffs, import taxes will rise significantly, with China facing up to 40% when the new duties take effect next year. According to the BBC, some of the rates will be reduced because of tariff caps that US President Donald Trump has already agreed to, and individual countries could also face different levies. What does this mean for gaming hardware? Trump's first round of "Liberation Day" tariffs contributed to rising console prices, but the Supreme Court eventually struck them down. Substantial companies like Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo benefited from tariff refunds after the ruling, but they didn't pass the savings on to consumers. In Sony's case, it was estimated to get back $508 million in refunds from the US government. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4FatSqS3VYY&t=19s The new tariffs bypass the Supreme Court's ruling by using a different law, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the government to impose tariffs on countries that use unfair business practices. The law does require an investigation into specific trade practices before rates are set. If higher import taxes take effect, console companies could face much higher costs, and protecting their profits will likely mean consumers have to cover the difference. Nintendo, Sony, and Microsoft have moved much of their final assembly out of China and into Southeast Asia, especially Vietnam, to avoid earlier tariffs. However, key parts like batteries and power supplies still mostly come from China, and if tariffs on these parts rise, total production costs for consoles made outside China will go up even more. Some electronic goods could be exempt from tariffs, and manufacturers often stockpile inventory ahead of tariff deadlines to delay price changes. But with rising costs from the ongoing components shortage amid the AI boom and other global factors, console prices remain at risk. After the June announcement of steep console price hikes, Microsoft warned that Xbox console costs could rise again in 2027, and next-gen hardware is also expected to be very pricey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as the workday progresses, you face small problems. Your phone is almost dead, with no charger in sight. You can’t find the piece of paper with yesterday’s meeting notes.

None of these small concerns necessitates a complete office makeover. Sometimes you just need a small upgrade to make life easier, like a charging station for your devices, a lamp that puts light where you need it or a voice recorder that transcribes meetings for you.

Black Friday is one of the best times to shop for office technology. The right purchase can remove everyday irritations — or simply make your workspace more pleasant — at a discounted price.

Can potential clients find you using AI?

📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing.
  • A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.”  If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online. Maybe you even track the information by asking or through a “How did you find me?” question on your website. Many people now ask an AI chatbot for a recommendation, the same way they’ve typed questions into Google for years. No matter how you feel about using AI tools personally, AI search is something that may have more and more of an impact on your business over time. AI as the latest recommendation engine For a long time, getting found online meant search engine optimization (SEO), or showing up in Google results by publishing content like a blog. The newer version is AEO (answer engine optimization) or GEO (generative engine optimization). The idea is that AI tools might “find” you the way Google once did. AEO and SEO share the same fundamentals. AI tools pull from publicly available information on the Internet, so the more you put out there, the easier you are to find. In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey, 45% of consumers said they used ChatGPT or another AI tool to get recommendations for local businesses. A year earlier, it was 6%. That’s a massive jump in a single year. The survey looked at local businesses, so it may not line up exactly with the work you do, but directionally it suggests that more and more people are turning to AI search to find what they’re looking for. Make sure you have a consistent online presence Like Google, AI tools look for an authoritative answer to whatever question someone asks. SEO has long focused on ranking in Google by following a set of “rules.” To me, AEO feels more like a wide-open, unclaimed field. No one quite understands it yet, though many people are trying to influence the AI search results. You can’t control the algorithms or LLMs, but you can control some of the narrative when Google Search or AI search finds you. AI tools piece together a description of you from all of these sources. Your website Your website is an obvious source for who you are and what you do. Your About and Products/ Services pages are good places to start. Make sure they’re up to date with the information you’d want someone to know or find. From there, you might add content that answers the questions potential clients are likely to ask. My website includes an FAQs section to help the algorithms and LLMs understand me better. Content also increases the likelihood that you’ll appear in search results, AI or otherwise. A blog works, and so does a publicly available newsletter. Case studies and testimonials help too, especially when they include client names and outcomes (with permission, of course). Your content on other sites Content on other sites gives AI tools something to cite when it answers someone’s question. It might be a podcast episode where you were a guest, or an article you wrote for someone else’s website. YouTube videos and social media posts count as well. Claim your business profile Google Business Profile is the original way to claim your business and correct its information. It’s worth setting up if you serve a local area, but for many online service providers (like me) it wasn’t necessary. In November 2026, OpenAI debuted a beta of Businesses in ChatGPT, which lets a business claim and manage its listing. It’s in beta and open to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S. Once your business is verified, you can upgrade its details. You’ll even be able to see how often ChatGPT mentions your business in its answers and how many people click through to your website. A LinkedIn Organization Page works for a one-person business, too. I have one, and it reveals up when people search on LinkedIn. AI is one more way people ask for information I’ll admit: I immediately claimed my business profile in ChatGPT when I heard it was available. It only took a few minutes to verify my website and identity, and then I could see what ChatGPT “knows” about me. I also plan to track how many times ChatGPT mentions me (at the moment sitting at 19). Word of mouth still keeps my pipeline full, because people know the type of work I do. But I can’t ignore that people are also turning to AI chatbots for recommendations.

GTA VI’s pretentious puzzler makes indie developers feel ‘part of larger culture’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and substantial-budget blockbusters.
  • Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and substantial-budget blockbusters.
  • One of the most intriguing games of the year is called Tenebrae Lux.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and substantial-budget blockbusters.

Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and substantial-budget blockbusters.

One of the most intriguing games of the year is called Tenebrae Lux. It’s a moody, black-and-white title with obtuse puzzles and a main character that constantly narrates to himself with dramatic language. Its credits attribute pretty much everything to a developer named Johannes Zuch. It’s generated a lot of discussion for seemingly mocking games like Jonathan Blow’s The Witness or The Chinese Room’s Dear Esther. It’s also a game that only exists inside of Grand Theft Auto VI.

Developer Rockstar Games has stuffed a lot of satirical media inside of GTA VI, including TV highlights you can watch, books you can read, and radio shows you can listen to. It’s all in service of making the world feel like a funhouse-mirror version of our current reality — Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis plays a right-wing radio host, for example. There are more games you can play inside GTA VI in addition to Tenebrae Lux, including a zombie-themed roguelike. But Tenebrae Lux, which you have to see as part of GTA VI’s main story, is the one that has struck a chord, including with indie developers like Sam Barlow and Robert Yang.

“I have to admit it’s kind of funny for the biggest blockbuster game of all time to go after arthouse indie,” Yang tells The Verge, noting that it’s “like a fighter jet getting obsessed with an ant, petty in a funny way.” (Given that GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day, the gulf between Rockstar and indie game studios that are struggling to get by is vast.).

It has been revealed that but Yang suggested that Rockstar developers are probably well versed in the types of games they’re lampooning in GTA VI. “I don’t think gamers understand how much indie experimental stuff any decent AAA dev plays,” Yang noted, pointing out that Rockstar’s environmental artists and level designers “all probably love Dear Esther,” the influential first-person game that helped popularize the “walking sim” concept when it launched in 2012.

“I was mostly taken with what it meant that the millions of people playing the game were having to sit down and play through an extended gag about indie games,” Barlow tells The Verge. “That made me feel like we were part of larger culture.” He added that he hopes some of these players might “seek out what these arty indie games might be.”.

Rockstar is self-aware enough to use its video games to poke fun at the medium itself. As part of a long conversation between protagonist Jason Duval and his friend Cal Hampton before they start playing Tenebrae Lux, Cal hypes the game by saying that none of it is “just sitting around waiting for people to finish talking.” Initially, you only play Tenebrae Lux for a few minutes, which is enough time to get stumped on the initial puzzles, before the game cuts back to Jason being bored. “Got anything else, a little less, uh… y’know?” he asks. They play the zombie game, titled Street Trash 3 Dezombifier, right after. (You can go back and play the entirety of Tenebrae Lux later if you want.).

According to recent reports, barlow said that the cut “felt very true to the character and story. I gather there is more to the game, but it felt natural to me to hit a wall with the pretentious puzzle design and then move on!”.

In a recent development, yang also pointed out that from a design perspective, GTA VI has more in common with Tenebrae Lux than Street Trash 3 Dezombifier. GTA VI is “basically a walking sim where you walk around Florida and listen to people talk,” Yang mentioned. “What’s the difference? Well, just like a billion dollars I guess.”.

Speaking to Vulture, Shoaibi mentioned she's able to see "more good than bad" thanks to her experience being a content creator. "There are weirdos out there, and they’re going to try to bring you down, so it’s crucial to stay around the people and the places that aren’t doing that," she said. "It’s easy enough to do, which I’m very grateful for. There’s enough support in my real-life community and online that I can say, 'I could just hang out over here. I don’t actually need to go to the scary place.' I’m living in the positive, for sure." https://www.youtube.com/shorts/JSJwQthWrZs People have been, to put it mildly, thirsting over Mandy since GTA 6 came out. However, Shoaibi had no idea she was going to be in GTA 6 at all because when she auditioned, she signed what she described as an "incredibly" strict NDA. Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced.
  • If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after fresh tools and processes have been introduced.
  • Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced. Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar. A new report by online learning platform TalentLMS, based on a survey of 1,500 US employees who had received training on a new tool, technology, process, or way of working in the previous 12 months, found that 65% of respondents mentioned letting go of an old habit is harder than learning a new one. And only 41% consistently used a new way of working after they were trained on it. Meanwhile, 42% admitted they still used tools or processes their managers believed had been replaced. Multiple industries are evolving and being disrupted by AI. Habit hugging could be a response to the pressure employees feel to continually adapt as everything changes around them. As uncertainty grows both inside and outside the office, sticking to what you know may offer a little comfort. There’s a tension between employers demanding adaptability and employees being expected to maintain productivity throughout that change: The report found that 48% of respondents felt rushed to adopt new ways of working. Employers aren’t necessarily helping their workforce overcome their old habits when they expect them to adopt new systems without slowing down or making mistakes. That pressure may also make employees reluctant to admit they’re struggling. The report found that 45% of respondents had avoided questioning a new way of working because they didn’t want to appear resistant. Among those who continued to use, or fell back on, old ways of working, 22% said they feared making mistakes or looking slow. When workplaces demand this constant adaptation without creating the space for it, employees might prefer to stick to what they know. Sixty percent said their workplace prioritized results over the process of getting them, while just 41% said they felt they were given room to be less productive while learning something new. There may also be a question of trust. Employees who have seen workplace initiatives and technologies come and go may be reluctant to embrace the latest change, particularly if they aren’t convinced it will last. They may prefer to future-proof themselves by leaning on the skills and systems they already know, rather than investing time in learning a new tool that could be forgotten about in six months. That reluctance could be costing employers: The report found that 29% of employees said their company was investing in tools they’d stopped using. But habit hugging isn’t necessarily an outright rejection of change. The report found that 73% of respondents mixed old and new ways of working to get the job done, suggesting employees may be finding ways to adapt without abandoning familiar routines altogether. Rather than blindly embracing the latest systems, people may be finding their own ways of adapting to a future nobody is sure of.

Latest Update: Diablo 4 Is Making Helltides A Hell Of A Lot Easier

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Gamespot)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Diablo 4's oldest endgame activities, Helltides, is getting a major refresh for Season 16.
  • One of Diablo 4's oldest endgame activities, Helltides, is getting a major refresh for Season 16.
  • As detailed by developer Blizzard in their full breakdown of Season of Tyrael's Gambit, Helltides will soon be far more efficient to run than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Diablo 4's oldest endgame activities, Helltides, is getting a major refresh for Season 16. As detailed by developer Blizzard in their full breakdown of Season of Tyrael's Gambit, Helltides will soon be far more efficient to run than before. The whole point of the activity is to kill as many demons as fast as possible, acquire the Aberrant Cinders they drop, and then use those cinders to open chests for items. Dying means losing half of the cinders you've collected, but they are also lost when the Helltide ends. Oftentimes that means having left over amounts of cinders you can't spend, only to then go to the next Helltide five minutes later and repeat the process from zero. It's been this way since Diablo 4 released back in 2023. https://www.youtube.com/live/zhsLeug_ooo?si=EeprZXb-pEZ_KRiQ In Season 16, that will finally change. Blizzard is getting rid of the downtime between Helltides spawning and making it so there will always be a Helltide up in one of the game's original zones, as well as one in expansion areas like Hahantu or Skovos. Even better, Aberrant Cinders won't be lost once a Helltide ends. Instead, players can collect up to 5,000 cinders at a time to be spent on opening chests within the activity. Additionally, the overall loot quality from opening chests in the Helltide will be improved and chests can be opened instantly. Those changes should go a long way towards making Helltides feel more valuable and efficient when trying to farm gear, as you can now blast demons to your heart's content until reaching the Aberrant Cinder cap. Just don't die while you have a full 5,000 stored up. Diablo 4 Season 16 debuts December 1. Alongside its Helltide changes, the season will bring big updates to War Intends as well. A newly introduced system, War Plans Tactics, will give players more control over what activities appear in their War Plans, as well as more options when it comes to rerolling them and the rewards they grant. Players will also have new Horadric items to chase that will modify specific Talisman sets, greatly increasing their power. Blizzard additionally confirmed many of the features that were added as part of Diablo 4 Season 15, Hell's Legacy, will be made permanent. Those additions include the season's capstone dungeons, optional bosses like Moophisto, the Annihilus Seal, Hellfire Torch Charm, and the season's legacy Unique items like Stone of Jordan.

The M5 MacBook Air offers 512GB of storage, a 13-inch Retina display, and a 10-core CPU and 8-Core GPU with 16GB of unified memory that can take on pretty much all everyday tasks with ease.

Figma employee sues, alleging firm forced her to confront harassers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (TechCrunch)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Figma engineer is suing the design software firm and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.
  • It has been revealed that the lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S.
  • In a recent development, “Figma was my dream company for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Figma engineer is suing the design software firm and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.

It has been revealed that the lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints. Park, who joined Figma in 2022, alleges the company’s response damaged her career, compensation, and mental health. The lawsuit also alleges that Park, who is Asian, faced racial and gender discrimination, including performance criticism based on stereotypes that Asian women are meek, timid, and conflict-averse.

In a recent development, “Figma was my dream company for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed. “It was a place where I felt that I could level up in my career, working on a lot of really cool, interesting things at scale.”.

Sources indicate that park is seeking damages, a jury trial, and a court order prohibiting Figma from requiring employees who report harassment to confront their alleged harassers. She also wants the company to adopt and enforce a process for investigating harassment complaints promptly and confidentially.

Industry observers note that when reached for comment, a spokesperson for Figma stated, “Figma does not tolerate discrimination or harassment. Figma also does not tolerate extortion. These claims have no merit, and we will present the facts in court.”.

It has been revealed that park told TechCrunch she initially had faith in Figma’s complaint process, expecting that if she documented the alleged harassment and reported it to the right people, the organization would act. But as an engineer in a male-dominated field, Park told TechCrunch, “I don’t feel that they took me seriously throughout this process.”.

Park, who is still employed at Figma, joined its San Francisco office in October 2022. Within weeks, her onboarding mentor — a fellow engineer — asked her on a date and continued pursuing her after she declined, Park alleges. She initially feared reporting him, worrying that her manager would “dismiss her reports or view her as the problem,” according to the lawsuit.

Park says she tried to avoid her onboarding mentor. In early 2023, for example, she delayed choosing a work project until he had picked one. When her manager criticized her for not being a “team player,” Park explained that she was trying to avoid the colleague she accused of harassment, according to the suit.

Her manager allegedly dismissed her concerns, saying he had “met his wife at work too” and treating the behavior as “harmless flirtation.” When Park asked to be kept off projects with the onboarding mentor, HR allegedly instructed her to confront him directly about his behavior.

In a recent development, the lawsuit ties that response to Figma’s culture of direct feedback, which Park alleges Field established and enforced. It says the manufacturer’s People organization trains managers to direct employees, including those reporting harassment, to give feedback directly to the person involved.

In March 2023, her manager assigned him to a major project she was leading, despite her request to be separated from him. Park told her manager that she would “figure it out,” but alleges that having to work with him affected her performance. Her manager gave her a 2 out of 5 on her performance review, criticizing her for not speaking up enough or engaging with others and for lacking presence. Park was put on a coaching initiative, which she completed in late 2023.

Industry observers note that changing managers didn’t help, according to the lawsuit. Her second manager also refused to separate them, allegedly telling Park that someone at her level should be able to resolve conflicts with teammates and that separating them would be “avoiding the problem.” Like her previous manager, he allegedly pointed out that he had met his partner at work.

Park alleges the harassment continued throughout 2023.

In April 2024, she transferred to another team, a move she claims set back her career by resetting her performance and promotion timeline.

On her new team, which had more women, Park remarked she felt better and no longer had to work with her alleged harasser. Her performance reviews improved, but in late 2025, she alleges another incident of sexual harassment, this time by her new manager.

Recent findings suggest that the incident followed a night out for drinks with her wife and two teammates, including her manager. The next day, during a team lunch, the manager allegedly mentioned Park’s sex life had been discussed the previous evening. Park, who said no such conversation had occurred in her or her wife’s presence, felt “horrified and humiliated” by comments she believed fetishized queer relationships.

In a recent development, A colleague reported the comments to HR as sexual harassment, according to the suit. Weeks later, Park’s manager apologized in a Slack message, saying she didn’t recall what she had said. When Park sought HR’s guidance, she was again told to address the matter directly with her manager.

During their conversation, the manager allegedly became defensive, and the encounter left Park feeling “crushed, anxious, and vulnerable.” The manager also allegedly remarked she would never make such a comment because she had “a lot of gay friends.”.

The manager told HR that they had agreed it was a misunderstanding. HR closed its investigation without interviewing witnesses, according to the suit, even though Park disputed her manager’s account.

“Requiring an employee to confront her harasser as the price of complaining — and then closing her complaint — would dissuade a reasonable employee from complaining at all,” the suit said.

Recent findings suggest that park alleges her manager retaliated by publicly berating her, sometimes so aggressively that colleagues intervened or checked on her afterward, according to the lawsuit. The suit also alleges that other teammates left the team over concerns about the manager’s behavior.

Park again complained to HR about “escalating retaliation” and expressed concern the manager would “derail her career.” HR allegedly defended the manager’s conduct, saying the manager was “within her reasonable authority” and again instructed Park to address her concerns directly with the manager.

In early 2026, Park received another low performance review and a reduced bonus. The lawsuit alleges that similarly situated men continued to receive promotions, raises, and bonuses. When Park reported the negative performance review to HR in March, she was allegedly told her sexual harassment complaint against her manager could not be “substantiated.”.

In a recent development, park took medical leave in March to receive treatment for PTSD symptoms and generalized anxiety. Cleared to return to work in June, she was prescribed workplace accommodations, including a graduated work schedule and mandatory remote workdays.

According to recent reports, park told TechCrunch that Figma approved the accommodations but had not implemented them at the time she returned to work. In July, Park and her lawyers notified Figma of their intent to pursue legal action.

According to recent reports, “It’s really scary for me,” she mentioned about taking legal action. “I don’t know what’s going to happen next with this, I don’t know what the outcome is going to be, but at least it feels like this is my chance to do the right thing.”.

This piece was updated to clarify when Park said Figma implemented the recommendations from her medical professionals.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that inflation remains stubborn. Producer prices are now running at a 6.5% annual clip, and affordability is top of mind. Want to cut some costs in your business? Of course you do. Try these moves.

Both ChatGPT and Claude offer connections to your bank account and credit card services. Or, if you’re nervous about that, just upload your statements. You’ll be impressed by the number of suggestions they make to reduce your spending and better manage expenses.

I used to think canceling online subscriptions would be a big headache, and years ago it was. Not anymore. Search for “cancel my subscription on Google Play” (or Apple or Amazon), and you’ll get direct links to do it. I’m betting you and your business have subscriptions you’ve forgotten about that are eating up hundreds of dollars a year.

Industry observers note that every year, put your business and auto insurance policies out for a quote. Ask your AI chatbot to make suggestions too. This is not very time-consuming and can be accomplished using an administrative person in your office. We’re oftentimes too lazy to do this. And that’s costing us.

Many of my clients have complicated, expensive coffee machines in their break rooms with a wide variety of coffees. They also stock sugar packets, teas, mini creamers, plastic stirrers and paper cups. It’s too much. Offer fewer coffees so you order less. Put out a sugar bowl, bring in a gallon of creamer and go back to ceramic mugs. Call me Scrooge, but it saves money.

NerdWallet does a great job regularly reviewing business and personal credit cards. Again, use your AI chatbot to look at your spending and tell it your preferences and you’ll get plenty of recommendations too. Moving to a better card could earn you more points and cashback rewards then you’re getting right now. I have some clients that regularly switch back and forth.

Industry observers note that speaking of credit, if your business buys products on Amazon, then make sure you use one of Amazon’s credit cards for purchases. With a Prime membership, you can earn 5% back on eligible Amazon purchases, and there’s no annual fee.

It has been revealed that if you can’t pay off a credit card purchase right away from operations, consider using working capital or a lower-rate loan to reduce the balance. Credit card interest rates are high, so this can cut what you pay in interest significantly.

This is a very common tax move, yet so many of us ignore it. Put as much as you can into your retirement initiative to lower your tax bill this year. When you save – assuming you’re eligible – sock money into a Roth IRA or Roth 401K so your after-tax money grows tax-free. With a Roth, there are no minimum distributions, and you can take the money out whenever you want, provided it meets certain requirements like a first-time home purchase, higher education or unreimbursed medical expenses.

According to recent reports, make sure your company has an HSA and contribute the max. It will reduce your tax expense and allow you to save money for future healthcare expenses.

Every square foot your inventory takes up costs you in overhead and space. Twice a year, take a hard look at your inventory and get rid of what isn’t moving. Sell it on Craigslist, eBay or Facebook Marketplace or scrap it.

Mark Cuban’s Cost Plus Drugs and Amazon Pharmacy both offer options that let businesses provide discounted prescription drugs, and they work with many popular health plans.

It has been revealed that set up a donor-advised fund and contribute to it this year, even if you haven’t decided which charities or nonprofits will receive the money. You take the deduction now and choose the recipients later.

I like Capital One Shopping. Add it as a browser extension for yourself and anyone else who makes purchases for your business. Whenever someone is on a shopping site, it searches for available coupons before you buy. It works about half the time, and it has saved me significant money over the years.

We can all afford the things we want — it’s just that sometimes we choose to spend our money on other things instead. That’s fine. But know that cutting back on things like travel, entertainment, subscriptions, marketing or other discretionary spending in your business (and your personal life) can help you reallocate your cash for other purposes. You’re more in control than you think.
